A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same self-play Q-learning study of the iterated prisoner's dilemma. The text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–E are readable and can be matched across the reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original tabular Q-learning simulations in Figures 1–3 and a five-run deep Q-learning experiment in Figure 4 and Appendix E.

after.justification: v2 retains these simulations and adds initialization comparisons in Figure 2 and payoff-incentive experiments in Figure 6 and Appendix E.1.

M1.justification: Both retain shared-table, one-step-memory, epsilon-greedy Q-learning and the same DQN procedure with random-opponent pretraining followed by self-play. v2 expands the pseudocode and initialization explanation without establishing a different learning procedure; the tightened initialization conditions concern the theoretical guarantees.

E1.justification: Appendix E.1 and Figure 6 extend evaluation to payoff environments with g = 1.75, 1.85, and 1.9 alongside the existing g = 1.8 case. Coverage remains within the same self-play iterated prisoner's dilemma task.

E2.justification: No evaluated comparison method is added or removed. The new grim-trigger entry in v2 Table 2 classifies a theoretical strategy; it is not an additional experimental baseline.

E3.justification: Figure 2 adds controlled runs with different initial Q-values while retaining the other Figure 1 settings. v2 also states that all experiments use gamma = 0.6, although its retained DQN hyperparameter table still specifies 0.8; whether the DQN setting actually changed is therefore unresolved.

E4.justification: v2 adds two focused sensitivity checks: Figure 2 compares initializations satisfying none, only the first, or all initialization conditions, while Appendix E.1 examines how payoff incentive g affects cooperation timing. The existing exploration and learning-rate analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both report 100-run means and standard-deviation shading for stochastic Q-learning trajectories, 100-run cooperation frequencies, and five DQN runs with individual curves and their mean. The added fully greedy analyses introduce no new uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: New results show failure to reach Pavlov for the tested insufficiently optimistic initializations and earlier cooperation transitions as g increases. The original trajectory results, cooperation-rate heatmap, and DQN results are retained; the additions do not establish a same-setting performance improvement.

T1.justification: Assumption 3.1 adds initial-Q inequalities absent from Assumption 7. v2 corrects the exploration-event bound and binomial-tail argument, adds an explicit O(1/alpha) derivation, and revises grim-trigger's equilibrium classification. Theorem 3.3 also changes the alternative outcome from win-stay to lose-shift and declares its constant independent of parameters on which v1's Theorem 9 said it depended. These substantially revise the central formal results.

C1.justification: v1 advertises the existence of new cooperative equilibria as a contribution. v2 treats these fixed points as established background and focuses its contributions on convergence from optimistic initialization. The central claims of learning Pavlov through self-play and observing cooperation with DQN remain.

C2.justification: v2 explains why controlling optimistic initialization is difficult with randomly initialized neural networks. It also expands the existing self-play limitation by discussing strategy switching without self-play and the need to analyze a stationary distribution, citing prior results rather than presenting a new experiment.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly supplies alpha = 0.1 for Figures 1–3, adds payoff and discount settings to trajectory captions, and spells out each player's state input in Algorithm 1. The DQN hyperparameter values, RTX8000 hardware, three-hour runtime per run, and absence of supplied code-access instructions remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 substantially revises attribution and positioning: Usui and Ueda (2021) and Meylahn and Janssen (2022) establish the fixed-point background that v1 presented as a contribution. The introduction and related work also expand coverage of empirical pricing evidence, decentralized learning, and learning-dynamics analyses.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, and Section 2 is reorganized around reinforcement learning, self-play, and established fixed points. The former new-equilibria subsection becomes background, appendices A and B exchange their subject matter, and an impact statement replaces the earlier checklist. The title now explicitly identifies self-play.

P2.justification: v2 adds two multipanel figures, redesigns and moves the policy table into the main text, and introduces a symbolic main-text payoff matrix while relocating the parameterized matrix to Appendix E. Existing plots receive limited axis-label, caption, and placement changes, and the document is reformatted in the ICML layout.

improvement.justification: The tightened assumptions, corrected probability argument, improved attribution, and added sensitivity checks provide useful gains. However, v2's Theorem 3.3 newly declares a parameter-independent constant while Appendix D.2 only argues independence from alpha; its Pavlov-or-lose-shift conclusion also conflicts with the win-stay alternative retained in Appendix D.3. These unresolved changes affect the main guarantee, preventing a reliable judgment of net overall improvement.
